item.title: Sam Altman says it's "quite terrible" that people use RAM in their PCs for AI during a shortage
item.itunes:title: Sam Altman says it's "quite terrible" that people use RAM in their PCs for AI during a shortage
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • AI demand is driving up RAM costs, making consumer sticks pricier.
  • Altman implies underused PC RAM should be in cloud data centers for higher utilization in an interview.
  • His remarks suggest a preference for cloud over consumer RAM, which shows a worrying trend if true.

If you've been RAM shopping any time in the last year or so, you've probably noticed that memory costs quite a bit more than it used to. Part of the reason is due to the increase in RAM usage for AI, as companies purchase large batches of sticks to cover their needs. Now, Sam Altman has gone on record saying that it's "quite terrible" that some of the limited amount of RAM in the world are in people's PCs.

People using the RAM in their PCs 5% of the time is "quite terrible," says OpenAI's Sam Altman

It was from a "global allocation perspective," but it's still a worrying one

Over in an interview on the Cheeky Pint (via IGN), Sam Altman discussed the current state of RAM. In the interview, he brings up that people want to run open-source AI on their own hardware. However, according to Altman, that's not a great thing:

From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer, and being used maybe 5% of the time. Like, you want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that.

It seems his point was that, in a shortage, he would prefer RAM in data centers where it'll be put to task for hours in a day, rather than someone's computer where it'll only be used a fraction of the time. And from a "global allocation perspective," I can see what he means.

But overall, I feel his statement has partially shown his hand and disposition toward consumers, particularly the last sentence: "And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that." I got the feeling that he thinks RAM sticks in his data centers are worth more than the RAM in people's PCs, whether they run AI off them or not. As if people should allow OpenAI to have the lion's share of RAM so that it can run more powerful AI models in the cloud. And that really comes off poorly in my eyes.

Regardless, this is just inference and speculation from a single interview, and it's not indicative of OpenAI's entire stance around the RAM shortage. However, I'd be lying if I said it didn't worry me at least a little bit.

The 16GB gaming PC is officially dead and current RAM pricing proves it

32GB has become the new minimum and my testing proved it for me.

15
By  Jasmine Mannan

item.title: Epic's Linux anti-cheat wants TPM 2.0 and a stack of settings, and you can check your own PC in about five minutes
item.itunes:title: Epic's Linux anti-cheat wants TPM 2.0 and a stack of settings, and you can check your own PC in about five minutes
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When Windows 11 arrived on the block, people running Windows 10 with older hardware hit a brick wall. Windows 11 requires a CPU with TPM 2.0, and if yours didn't have it, you had to perform workarounds just to get it installed. The alternative was to move to Linux, where TPM 1.2 chips were supported, and still are.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Unfortunately, it appears even Linux isn't totally free from TPM shenanigans. If you love competitive gaming, Epic Games' Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) version 2 will require you to have a TPM 2.0 chip to play its games.

Epic Games' Easy Anti-Cheat didn't play nicely with Linux at all...

It was causing some real issues for Linux gamers

Before we hop into what EAC v2 brings, we have to take a look at the first version. EAC is a kernel-level anti-cheat that Epic Games uses to ensure people don't cheat in its popular online games, like Fortnite. Deploying kernel-level anti-cheat is just fine when the kernel in question is locked down and proprietary, like Windows'. It's not so great when using it on an OS where the kernel is open-source, and anyone can tinker with it, like Linux's.

EAC’s relationship with Linux has been pretty rough. Epic didn't completely ignore it; after all, we saw native support arrive in 2014, and Proton/Wine compatibility in 2021. But because these ran in the user space and weren't locked-down kernel drivers, Epic made them optional.

Unsurprisingly, most developers took the simplest route to prevent Linux-based cheaters: saying no to Linux entirely. When you're trying to run a competitive multiplayer online game, ruining its reputation just so a smattering of players on CachyOS can play is more trouble than it's worth, which is why even Epic kept Fortnite off Linux. Well, the good news is, Epic Games found a way to include Linux, but people with older hardware won't be too fond of it.

I stopped fighting anti-cheat on Linux and started using Steam Remote Play, and I don't miss dual-booting

If I can't completely escape Windows, I can just offload it onto something else

4
By  Ty Sherback

...but v2 will allow some Linux gamers in if they have the hardware

Better than nothing, I suppose

On October 14th, Epic Games posted a blog detailing its plans for Linux. It'll release what it calls EAC Linux v2, and the objective is to bring "the level of protection much closer to par with Windows, in the very near term." To do this, it will use existing Linux features to get the job done.

While it won't use a kernel module like Windows, it will need a laundry list of hardware. For starters, you need to be using a distro with a signed kernel. Your PC needs Secure Boot enabled, and your boot loader needs to have Measured Boot. You also need IOMMU, Kernel Lockdown Integrity Mode, and the Linux Security Module BPF all enabled, and Kexec, a feature that lets you load a new kernel without rebooting, must be disabled.

However, one entry on the list will bring back bad Windows 11 memories:

TPM 2.0 is standard on modern consumer hardware, and software support is built into the Linux kernel. We require that systems have TPM 2.0 support and that it is enabled in the BIOS.

Epic Games cites TPM 2.0's technologies like Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs) as the reason why it's demanding it, claiming it allows for a "tamper-resistant boot log to be produced and verified." This should allow EAC Linux v2 to look at what code ran during boot without needing to actually run at boot. However, it does mean that TPM 1.2 users are left behind.

There is some good news, such as EAC Linux v2 being a systemd service that only loads when a protected game boots up and closes when it's finished. But it's not ideal for anyone who uses Linux because of its older hardware compatibility. One could argue that someone with a PC that fails these tests probably isn't playing competitive games anyway, but it is confirmed in the blog post's FAQ section that the Steam Deck is still left high and dry for compatibility.

Linux is now adopting a CPU requirement Windows already demands, but don't worry, it's not TPM 2.0

In fact, if you're reading this line, your computer's CPU is most definitely still supported.

7
By  Simon Batt

Giving your Linux a quick check-up is simple

You just need to run a few commands

To see whether your Linux PC fits the bill, run these quick commands. They'll let you know if your PC passes at least five of the eight requirements:

  • Secure Boot: mokutil --sb-state should say it's enabled.
  • TPM 2.0: cat /sys/class/tpm/tpm0/tpm_version_major reporting a "2" means you have TPM 2.0. A "1" means you're on TPM 1.2.
  • Kernel Lockdown: cat /sys/kernel/security/lockdown must show [integrity]for it to be valid.
  • BPF LSM: cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm must include bpfto prove compatibility.
  • Kexec: cat /proc/sys/kernel/kexec_load_disabled must output 1.
Nvidia’s RTX Spark passed most of my anti-cheat tests, but Valorant and Call of Duty still won’t run (yet)

Anti-cheat support from Riot Games, CoD, and EA are in the works

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Gaming on Linux is getting easier, for some

All things considered, I'm grateful Epic Games is doing something to allow more Linux gamers to play online. I just wish it didn't have to include the shadow of Windows 11's system requirements.

item.title: I stopped paying for Lightroom after finding a free open-source editor that handles my RAW files just as well
item.itunes:title: I stopped paying for Lightroom after finding a free open-source editor that handles my RAW files just as well
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The industry standard for working with RAW files has been Adobe Lightroom for nearly two decades, but being tied down to a subscription has left myself and many other users with a bad taste in our mouths. Paying every month for software I mostly use for product shots has always felt like renting a screwdriver, and the free alternatives all had their own unique workflow that I didn't want to adopt in full.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

LightCraft is the first one I've come across that doesn't force me to change my workflow but also has most of the features I use daily. It's very young and was made with some heavy assistance from Claude Opus, so there are some places where it doesn't match Adobe, but for the way I shoot, it's the perfect replacement.

An open-source Adobe suite built with AI is almost ready to replace the real thing

ArtCraft has seriously impressed me

6
By  Ty Sherback

It feels like Lightroom, which is so important

I'm not re-learning how to import and edit photos with LightCraft

I primarily shoot product shots on my iPhone 18 Pro, but on occasion, I do shoot on a Rebel T3i, which give me 14-bit CR2 files. These are a very common older format that could trip up a newer piece of software if it's not configured correctly, but LightCraft imports them easily, and has supported them from its earliest working build. The project has since checked decoded CR2 files from a long list of Canon bodies against each one's own JPEG, so it's got pretty good support for them.

The file import process is very similar to Lightroom, and once the files are in, editing them feels very natural. Exposure, white balance, tone curves, masking, cropping and upright perspective correction sit roughly where a Lightroom user would expect them, and every change made to the photo is stored as an edit rather than written into the original file. Presets, version history and copying settings across a batch also work the way they do in Lightroom.

RapidRAW is the free, open-source Lightroom alternative I've been waiting for

Editing photos is about to get a whole lot easier

8
By  João Carrasqueira

It ditches the parts of Lightroom that make Adobe apps a pain

No subscription, compatibility with Linux, and completely open-source

I think the thing that has me truly hooked onto LightCraft is the bits that aren't technical, though. Lightroom's primary lock-in is years of habit, and thankfully, LightCraft doesn't make any statements with its design or UI. It's trying to be 1:1 for the stuff you'll use in the app, and it ditches most of the annoying things that make Adobe apps painful to use.

LightCraft is completely free and open-source, which is huge for an app that feels so close to a first-party Adobe app. Everything runs locally on Windows, macOS, and even Linux, which is a bonus for someone like me who doesn't want to constantly switch devices from the Linux machine I'm writing on to edit photos. It's also really fast to boot up and feels snappy to click around in—I didn't notice any slowdowns while editing or scrolling through my library.

6 reasons Darktable is better than Adobe Lightroom for hobbyist photo editors

Why pay for Lightroom when Darktable does more?

7
By  Nolen Jonker

Where it still falls short of Adobe Lightroom

LightCraft won't be a complete replacement for many

Color is by far the biggest gap between LightCraft and Lightroom, and it's not particularly close. Adobe ships tuned profiles for an enormous range of cameras, including Camera Matching profiles that mimic each body’s in-camera looks. LightCraft can’t use those. It relies on data stored in DNG files, its own fitted profiles for a handful of cameras, and look estimates built from camera JPEGs for certain formats. Older CR2 files like mine aren’t on that list, so they start from a more neutral rendering.

Lens correction is another place where it falls behind a bit. Lightroom matches thousands of lens profiles automatically, while LightCraft only applies the corrections that the camera wrote into the file itself. My camera doesn't produce a format it can read those from, so things like distortion and vignetting on my kit lens are manual adjustments I have to make.

AI features like masking and denoise are still in progress, but there is the ability to load a local model to perform some actions within LightCraft. Subject and sky selection use more traditional detection rather than an AI model, while object selection and AI denoise both depend on optional local models you install yourself. AI Denoise also only works on traditional Bayer-sensor RAW files for now, so it won’t touch my iPhone’s ProRAW shots. I haven’t tested how well the local tools perform myself.

I tried replacing Photoshop, Lightroom, and Acrobat with free vibe-coded alternatives, and they're surprisingly good

Got to give credit where credit's due

10
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Where familiar still beats the mature options

Lightroom refugees that perform the simple edits will be at home

Credit: 

Friction is such a large part of why LightCraft exists in the first place, and I think eliminating it is naturally going to pull a lot of users off of Lightroom and other FOSS options, even if it's not totally feature complete. For the average person editing some photos that their iPhone took in ProRAW or their older DSLR, the features are already there. The professional photographer will still need what Adobe offers, at least right now. And for them, the monthly investment in the software is absolutely worthwhile. Things like gaps in color profiles and lack of support for some formats just means it will be unusable for those kinds of users, but for the weekend photographer like me, it's perfect.

I replaced the Adobe suite with a free open source alternative that Claude can control directly

Artcraft clones Adobe's apps for free, and Claude can run them for you.

9
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Should you cancel your Adobe subscription?

Whether you should actually cancel your subscription depends on what camera you shoot with and what you actually use Lightroom for. If your body is well-supported, your edits are mostly global adjustments and presets, and you’re comfortable doing lens corrections by hand, LightCraft is already a credible free replacement, with seemingly more features on the way. If you depend on Adobe’s camera profiles, automatic lens corrections, AI denoise or mobile sync, I'd keep paying for now.

item.title: I gave ChatGPT Dots access to my email, calendar, and tasks, and it started helping without being asked
item.itunes:title: I gave ChatGPT Dots access to my email, calendar, and tasks, and it started helping without being asked
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Right now, the AI trend every company seems to be jumping on are always-on AI assistants that don't just wait around for you to give them instructions. OpenClaw helped kick off the craze for always-on AI assistants earlier this year. It wasn't long before major AI companies began experimenting with their own takes on the concept. Anthropic introduced Claude Dispatch, Meta launched Muse, and OpenAI eventually joined the party with ChatGPT Dots at its DevDay conference in September.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've been testing Dots for the last two weeks or so, and I've taken the bold step of connecting it to a bunch of tools I rely on daily. Turns out, the promise of having an AI assistant that proactively helps you without being asked isn't as far-fetched as I initially thought.

So, what even are ChatGPT Dots?

Think ChatGPT, but with a mind of its own

OpenAI describes Dots as always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra. Think of them as personal AI assistants that don't just sit around waiting for you to give them instructions. Instead, they can proactively look for ways to help you, keep track of ongoing tasks, and even get work done without you having to ask.

Dots can connect to the apps and services you already rely on through OpenAI's ecosystem of plugins. Once connected, they can keep an eye on what's happening across these apps, flag things that might need your attention, and help you stay on top of your responsibilities. They also learn your preferences over time, so ideally, the longer you work with your Dot, the better it gets at understanding what matters to you.

Note: Dots are currently limited to select paid plans, including ChatGPT Pro, which starts at a whopping $100 per month! OpenAI provided me with complimentary access to ChatGPT Pro to test the feature, but had no editorial input or influence over this article. All opinions expressed are my own.

Each Dot also gets its own cloud computer and browser, which means it can take on more complicated tasks without relying on your own device. You can assign it multiple projects, let it work on them simultaneously, and even close ChatGPT entirely while it continues working in the background. You can also view its computer to see what it's doing, or take over the controls yourself when needed.

Getting Dots connected to my digital life was surprisingly easy

A few clicks later, I had a personal assistant

The concept behind OpenClaw was so well-received for a good reason. Beyond the privacy concerns, though, one of its biggest drawbacks, especially when it first went viral, was the technical barrier to getting started. You needed to be comfortable running terminal commands, configuring AI models, and setting up integrations before you could really start using it.

Sure, none of this was necessarily impossible for someone with a technical background, but it wasn't exactly the kind of tool an average person could just open and start using, either. Dots eliminates much of this friction. If you're comfortable using ChatGPT for your everyday tasks, you can set up a Dot and begin using it. I'd argue that it's even simpler than that!

ChatGPT essentially walks you through the entire process. You give your Dot a name, customize its appearance, and choose which apps and services you want it to access. I connected mine to Gmail, Google Calendar, Asana, Slack, Notion, Outlook, and a few other tools I rely on daily.

The entire process took just a few minutes, and there were no terminal commands, API keys, or complicated configurations to worry about.

What I particularly like is how approachable OpenAI has made the entire experience. From the adorable little characters you can customize to the fact that interacting with your Dot feels just like having a regular ChatGPT conversation, there's very little about it that feels intimidating.

Dots started helping before I even asked

Dots understood the assignment before I gave it one

One of the biggest selling points of Dots is that they don't necessarily need you to tell them what to do. They're designed to proactively look for ways to help, and while I was initially a little skeptical about how useful that would actually be, it turned out to be one of my favorite things about the entire experience.

Before I'd even gotten around to assigning my Dot anything specific to monitor, it managed to surprise me. Let's just say I made a financial mistake that could've turned into a pretty expensive mess, a mere 40 minutes before I was supposed to leave for an exam. Perfect timing, right?

Naturally, I went into full panic mode. I turned to ChatGPT to find every customer support email address and phone number I could possibly use to get the transaction reversed. After sending an email and eventually getting through to customer support over the phone, there wasn't much else I could do. I had an exam to get to, so I put my phone away and hoped for the best.

When I finally got back, I noticed a notification from my Dot. It had spotted a response from customer support in my Gmail inbox, realized it was good news, and decided to let me know. Mind you, I hadn't asked it to monitor the situation, check for replies, or even explained much about what had happened in the first place.

Yes, I could've absolutely opened Gmail and read the email myself. In fact, that was the first thing I was going to do when I checked my phone, before I saw Dots' message. However, that's precisely what made this feel so different from using a regular AI chatbot. I wasn't the one initiating the interaction. Just as an actual assistant would have done, Dots recognized that something important had happened and took the initiative to bring it to my attention without me having to ask.

It didn't just stop there! Even after I had received a positive response from one customer support agent, Dots made sure to continue keeping me in the loop. At one point, there was some conflicting information from two customer support agents, and my Dot flagged that, too.

What impressed me even more is what happened as I was writing this article, when I made another withdrawal from the same account. Dots remembered the previous incident and proactively messaged me to check whether I'd actually intended to make this one. I hadn't asked it to keep an eye on my future transactions, either!

Another example happened when Dots noticed an email from my college about an upcoming tuition fee deadline. I'm supposed to be traveling next week, and the deadline happens to clash with the day I'm flying out. Missing it would mean paying a pretty hefty late fee.

Now, here's the funny part. I actually missed my tuition deadline last semester because I was traveling and ended up having to pay the late fee. So, having my Dot bring this to my attention before I made the same mistake again was genuinely helpful. These might seem like relatively small things, but I think that's precisely what makes the proactive element so useful.

Some tasks take much longer with Dots

Dots takes longer, but I don't always mind

One thing I noticed pretty quickly is that Dots isn't particularly fast. Even tasks that a regular ChatGPT conversation could handle in a fraction of the time sometimes take considerably longer. Judging by what other users have reported, on Reddit and other community forums, I'm certainly not alone in noticing this.

However, I've realized that speed isn't necessarily the most important thing when you're dealing with an AI assistant. What matters more to me is how much of my own time and attention I need to spend getting something done.

Remember how I mentioned that every Dot gets its own cloud computer? This is where that becomes particularly useful. Instead of having to sit around waiting for it to finish a task, I can simply assign it something, let it get to work in the background, and go about my day.

It can even work on multiple tasks simultaneously, without needing my laptop to do the heavy lifting. Rather than having to constantly check whether it's finished, my Dot can reach out with updates or let me know when something needs my attention.

For instance, at one point, I wanted to analyze some trends on Instagram. Rather than manually gathering the information or paying for a third-party connector, I simply logged into Instagram through my Dot's cloud browser and asked it to do the research for me.

While it was working on that, I gave it another task: building me a portfolio website. Both tasks were running in parallel, and I could check on their progress whenever I wanted. I could even open my Dot's cloud computer to see exactly what it was doing and take over the controls if needed.

Would I have gotten some of these results faster by using regular ChatGPT? Definitely. However, the fact that I could hand off two completely different tasks, continue with my own work, and check back when there was something worth looking at made the slower execution a lot easier to overlook.

My Dot and I have become phone buddies

I didn't expect to enjoy calling my Dot this much

I'm all for fun tech. I mean it! One of my favorite things I got to experience at IFA was HONOR's Robot Phone, and watching it dance along to some tunes and sing random songs was genuinely entertaining. Yes, that changes absolutely nothing about your life or mine, but the world is already serious enough. Does a little fun really hurt?

That's sort of how I feel about Dots' calling feature. You can actually hop on a voice call with your Dot and have a full-blown conversation. Surprisingly, the conversations feel fairly natural. My Dot laughs along when I laugh, pauses between sentences, and even throws in the occasional cough. It's almost eerily realistic at times, and while I can see why some people might find that a little creepy (I do too sometimes), it pretty cool.

Calling your Dot isn't just a novelty, though. Unlike having a regular voice conversation with ChatGPT, you're talking to an AI agent that can actually get work done on your behalf. You can bounce ideas back and forth, ask it to research something, or delegate an entirely new task without having to interrupt whatever you're doing. It can get to work in the background, spin up a separate task when needed, and report back with updates or results.

I used Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra to build the same portfolio — the difference was immediately obvious

Same prompt executed very differently

3
By  Nolen Jonker

I've found this especially useful when I'm already working on my laptop. I can keep the call running on my other screen, talk through whatever's on my mind, and have my Dot get started on things as they come up. It's a little like having an assistant sitting beside you, ready to take something off your plate whenever you think of it.

For instance, earlier this week, my Dot noticed some new assignments in Asana and brought them to my attention. With midterms approaching and a bunch of work commitments to juggle, I decided to hop on a call and ask it to help me organize my calendar. We spent a few minutes discussing my priorities, figuring out what needed to get done first, and deciding how best to time-block everything.

So, is Dots really worth it?

I do have to admit that I see the hype. But is it worth paying upwards of $100 per month for, at least right now? Not really.That said, Dots is still in its early days, and there's plenty of room for improvement.

For now, though, my experience has been a mixed bag, but a surprisingly positive one overall. Dots certainly hasn't replaced the way I use ChatGPT for everyday tasks, and I don't think it will anytime soon. However, having an AI assistant that remembers what matters to me, keeps an eye on things I might otherwise overlook, and occasionally takes the initiative to help without being asked? That's something I can absolutely get behind!

Right now, the AI trend every company seems to be jumping on are always-on AI assistants that don't just wait around for you to give them instructions. OpenClaw helped kick off the craze for always-on AI assistants earlier this year. It wasn't long before major AI companies began experimenting with their own takes on the concept. Anthropic introduced Claude Dispatch, Meta launched Muse, and OpenAI eventually joined the party with ChatGPT Dots at its DevDay conference in September.

I've been testing Dots for the last two weeks or so, and I've taken the bold step of connecting it to a bunch of tools I rely on daily. Turns out, the promise of having an AI assistant that proactively helps you without being asked isn't as far-fetched as I initially thought.

So, what even are ChatGPT Dots?

Think ChatGPT, but with a mind of its own

OpenAI describes Dots as always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra. Think of them as personal AI assistants that don't just sit around waiting for you to give them instructions. Instead, they can proactively look for ways to help you, keep track of ongoing tasks, and even get work done without you having to ask.

Dots can connect to the apps and services you already rely on through OpenAI's ecosystem of plugins. Once connected, they can keep an eye on what's happening across these apps, flag things that might need your attention, and help you stay on top of your responsibilities. They also learn your preferences over time, so ideally, the longer you work with your Dot, the better it gets at understanding what matters to you.

Note: Dots are currently limited to select paid plans, including ChatGPT Pro, which starts at a whopping $100 per month! OpenAI provided me with complimentary access to ChatGPT Pro to test the feature, but had no editorial input or influence over this article. All opinions expressed are my own.

Each Dot also gets its own cloud computer and browser, which means it can take on more complicated tasks without relying on your own device. You can assign it multiple projects, let it work on them simultaneously, and even close ChatGPT entirely while it continues working in the background. You can also view its computer to see what it's doing, or take over the controls yourself when needed.

Getting Dots connected to my digital life was surprisingly easy

A few clicks later, I had a personal assistant

The concept behind OpenClaw was so well-received for a good reason. Beyond the privacy concerns, though, one of its biggest drawbacks, especially when it first went viral, was the technical barrier to getting started. You needed to be comfortable running terminal commands, configuring AI models, and setting up integrations before you could really start using it.

Sure, none of this was necessarily impossible for someone with a technical background, but it wasn't exactly the kind of tool an average person could just open and start using, either. Dots eliminates much of this friction. If you're comfortable using ChatGPT for your everyday tasks, you can set up a Dot and begin using it. I'd argue that it's even simpler than that!

ChatGPT essentially walks you through the entire process. You give your Dot a name, customize its appearance, and choose which apps and services you want it to access. I connected mine to Gmail, Google Calendar, Asana, Slack, Notion, Outlook, and a few other tools I rely on daily.

The entire process took just a few minutes, and there were no terminal commands, API keys, or complicated configurations to worry about.

What I particularly like is how approachable OpenAI has made the entire experience. From the adorable little characters you can customize to the fact that interacting with your Dot feels just like having a regular ChatGPT conversation, there's very little about it that feels intimidating.

Dots started helping before I even asked

One of the biggest selling points of Dots is that they don't necessarily need you to tell them what to do. They're designed to proactively look for ways to help, and while I was initially a little skeptical about how useful that would actually be, it turned out to be one of my favorite things about the entire experience.

Before I'd even gotten around to assigning my Dot anything specific to monitor, it managed to surprise me. Let's just say I made a financial mistake that could've turned into a pretty expensive mess, a mere 40 minutes before I was supposed to leave for an exam. Perfect timing, right?

Naturally, I went into full panic mode. I turned to ChatGPT to find every customer support email address and phone number I could possibly use to get the transaction reversed. After sending an email and eventually getting through to customer support over the phone, there wasn't much else I could do. I had an exam to get to, so I put my phone away and hoped for the best.

When I finally got back, I noticed a notification from my Dot. It had spotted a response from customer support in my Gmail inbox, realized it was good news, and decided to let me know. Mind you, I hadn't asked it to monitor the situation, check for replies, or even explained much about what had happened in the first place.

Yes, I could've absolutely opened Gmail and read the email myself. In fact, that was the first thing I was going to do when I checked my phone, before I saw Dots' message. It didn't just stop there! Even after I had received a positive response from one customer support agent, Dots made sure to continue keeping me in the loop. At one point, there was some conflicting information from two customer support agents, and my Dot flagged that, too.

Dots remembered the previous incident and proactively messaged me to check whether I'd actually intended to make this one. I hadn't asked it to keep an eye on my future transactions, either!

Another example happened when Dots noticed an email from my college about an upcoming tuition fee deadline. I'm supposed to be traveling next week, and the deadline happens to clash with the day I'm flying out. Missing it would mean paying a pretty hefty late fee.

Now, here's the funny part. I actually missed my tuition deadline last semester because I was traveling and ended up having to pay the late fee. So, having my Dot bring this to my attention before I made the same mistake again was genuinely helpful. These might seem like relatively small things, but I think that's precisely what makes the proactive element so useful.

Some tasks take much longer with Dots

Dots takes longer, but I don't always mind

One thing I noticed pretty quickly is that Dots isn't particularly fast. Even tasks that a regular ChatGPT conversation could handle in a fraction of the time sometimes take considerably longer. Judging by what other users have reported, on Reddit and other community forums, I'm certainly not alone in noticing this.

However, I've realized that speed isn't necessarily the most important thing when you're dealing with an AI assistant. What matters more to me is how much of my own time and attention I need to spend getting something done.

Remember how I mentioned that every Dot gets its own cloud computer? This is where that becomes particularly useful. Instead of having to sit around waiting for it to finish a task, I can simply assign it something, let it get to work in the background, and go about my day.

It can even work on multiple tasks simultaneously, without needing my laptop to do the heavy lifting. Rather than having to constantly check whether it's finished, my Dot can reach out with updates or let me know when something needs my attention.

For instance, at one point, I wanted to analyze some trends on Instagram. Rather than manually gathering the information or paying for a third-party connector, I simply logged into Instagram through my Dot's cloud browser and asked it to do the research for me.

While it was working on that, I gave it another task: building me a portfolio website. Both tasks were running in parallel, and I could check on their progress whenever I wanted. I could even open my Dot's cloud computer to see exactly what it was doing and take over the controls if needed.

Would I have gotten some of these results faster by using regular ChatGPT? Definitely. However, the fact that I could hand off two completely different tasks, continue with my own work, and check back when there was something worth looking at made the slower execution a lot easier to overlook.

I didn't expect to enjoy calling my Dot this much

I'm all for fun tech. I mean it! One of my favorite things I got to experience at IFA was HONOR's Robot Phone, and watching it dance along to some tunes and sing random songs was genuinely entertaining. Yes, that changes absolutely nothing about your life or mine, but the world is already serious enough. Does a little fun really hurt?

That's sort of how I feel about Dots' calling feature. You can actually hop on a voice call with your Dot and have a full-blown conversation. Surprisingly, the conversations feel fairly natural. My Dot laughs along when I laugh, pauses between sentences, and even throws in the occasional cough. It's almost eerily realistic at times, and while I can see why some people might find that a little creepy (I do too sometimes), it pretty cool.

I do have to admit that I see the hype. But is it worth paying upwards of $100 per month for, at least right now? Not really.That said, Dots is still in its early days, and there's plenty of room for improvement.

For now, though, my experience has been a mixed bag, but a surprisingly positive one overall. That's something I can absolutely get behind!

item.title: AAA games are now playable in web browsers, and AI-assisted reverse engineering is the secret sauce
item.itunes:title: AAA games are now playable in web browsers, and AI-assisted reverse engineering is the secret sauce
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
AAA games becoming free-to-play right inside Chrome couldn't possibly have been on anyone's 2026 bingo card, but this year continues to deliver more strange news on the gaming front. Now, games that you'd otherwise find in your Steam library are available right in your browser, bringing a whole new dimension to "browser-based games."

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Browser games used to mean quick, non-committal, and often low-polygon games that you'd play once in a while to take a break from work. Now, however, some of the greatest games from the sixth and seventh generation of gaming are making their way to Chrome and Firefox, and all you need to do to play them is open a new tab and get going.

I remastered all my favorite PS3 games with DLSS 5, and I can't get enough

My PS3 collection is going from old to next-gen at light speed

14
By  Samarveer Singh

Full-blown AAA titles are running smoothly in-browser

I never thought I'd see the day

After an hour-long session of Call of Duty: Black Ops Zombies, I never thought that the way to close the game would be pressing Ctrl+W to close the tab in my browser window, yet here we are. Websites like ported2browser.com and wasm.rip are quite literally hosting major AAA titles, all a single click away. The projects don't take hours to download, either, as the assets stream quickly, as long as you have a fast internet connection.

I tried out every single game I grew up on, including Need for Speed: Most Wanted and Underground 2, Tekken 5, Smackdown vs Raw, Pro Evolution Soccer 2011, and so many more. It's astonishing just how quickly these games run, and how smoothly they play right inside the browser. One would assume that since these are proper AAA titles running inside a browser, even if the coding at the back of house is sound, they would still stutter or run at 10 fps or less, but I got a consistent 60 fps experience throughout, every single time.

Even the open-world games like Grand Theft Auto: Vice City and GTA III ran at a solid framerate, with medium-to-high graphics, all while only consuming about a gigabyte of my GPU VRAM and spiking GPU utilization by 10% or less. I may never have played Halo: Combat Evolved's original multiplayer when it came out, since I didn't even have a PC at the time, but there's a functional multiplayer version of the game online today, complete with a server browser as well. Even the entire campaign is ported to this web version, meaning I can play the game from start to finish, and all I need to do for that is open a new tab and get started.

AI-created gaming mod mashups are pure chaos, and I can't get enough of them

Tommy Vercetti is the new Tony Hawk

By  Samarveer Singh

Cyberpunk 2077 and GTA V ran at remarkable frame rates, too

The entirety of the GTA V campaign took a minute to load and start

While I was pleasantly surprised at just how smoothly the likes of genre-defining titles Resident Evil 4, Tekken 5, and Need for Speed: Most Wanted ran on my Chrome web browser, two games in particular caught my eye in the list of all the 285 titles on ported2browser.com. I couldn't possibly contain my shock at seeing Cyberpunk 2077 and Grand Theft Auto V both listed as playable, although the former did come with a note about being a work-in-progress with potential game-breaking bugs.

I started with GTA V, of course. Was it legal for Rockstar's entire game to be ported over to a web browser as a free-to-play game. Absolutely not. Was it absolutely shocking for the entire campaign to be up and running smoothly within a couple of minutes? Even more so. In fact, the game ran at a perfect 60 fps at graphics that looked like they belonged on a PlayStation 4 or even a PS4 Pro. Of course, my own GPU, the RTX 4070 Ti, was doing plenty of heavy lifting for the game, since GTA V in the browser required around 6–7 GB of VRAM, although utilization remained just 17%.

When the time came for Cyberpunk, the initial character creation menu bugged out with my character's face caving inwards and never fixing itself, but the moment I started the campaign, things were right as rain. Cyberpunk ran a little worse for wear, though, and I didn't manage to get a smooth 60 fps experience in CDPR's open-world RPG. Regardless, the game ran, and it ran well enough for Night City to look exactly like it did on my RTX 2070 Super PC all the way back in 2020, which, ironically, I'd built for that very game.

Bloodborne and P.T. finally run on PC "natively," so I remastered them with DLSS 5

These abandoned classics deserved better

2
By  Samarveer Singh

AI is making reverse-engineering a whole lot easier

Developers have more help today than ever before

So how is any of this becoming possible all of a sudden? We're not talking about stripped-down demos or cheap knock-offs, either — no "Call of Battlefield" or "Grand Auto Larceny" here. We're seeing genuine and legitimate attempts to bring entire commercial games, complete with their original gameplay systems, levels, and mechanics, to a platform they were never designed to run on.

The secret sauce here, of course, is AI-assisted reverse engineering. Solo developers are using coding agents like Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex to analyze compiled game code, reconstruct its underlying logic, and write replacement engines to replicate how the original games work.

With AI agents accelerating the work and doing the heavy lifting, the open-source community is flooding the internet with reverse-engineered game versions. In fact, they're even going a step further and decompiling titles from other platforms and rebuilding them to run natively on PC, creating ports and remasters we simply never thought would exist.

I gave my retro DOS games the DLSS 5 treatment, and the results were all over the place

Neural rendering in a retro gaming setup is interesting, to say the least.

1
By  Samarveer Singh

WebGPU and HTTPS developments are making this possible, too

All the right pieces are maturing at the same time

AI isn't doing all the heavy lifting from scratch, though. There are years of community-led decompilation projects and open-source engine reimplementations behind this, and they have already laid much of the groundwork.

The final piece of the puzzle that's making all of this possible is the maturation we're now seeing in WebAssembly. It lets developers run decompiled C and C++ code inside browsers, alongside web graphics technologies that handle rendering. Put that together with a deconstructed game engine, and that's how you get decade-old AAA games running in browser tabs without requiring an original console or a traditional PC installation.

There's also the fact that most of the world's browsers have become considerably stronger gaming platforms. The gradual adoption of WebGPU gives developers access to more modern graphics capabilities, making it easier to render demanding scenes without relying on traditional game installations.

Meanwhile, on-demand asset streaming over HTTPS means players don't necessarily have to download 20, 30, or even 50 GB of game files before getting started. Instead, compatible projects can fetch the assets they need over the internet as gameplay progresses. For players with fast, stable connections, this can dramatically reduce the wait between opening a browser tab and jumping into a game.

Moonlight and Apollo help me experience my PC games the console way

My PlayStation is shaking in terror

By  Samarveer Singh

Are these browser-based game ports even legal?

Reverse-engineering isn't the same as piracy

This is where we enter the grey, murky waters of legality. Speaking strictly in technical terms, reverse-engineering a game isn't illegal, and there are certain jurisdictions in the world where the laws permit it (under specific circumstances). However, copyright protection still applies to the original game's code, artwork, audio, and other assets.

That's why the decompilations of projects like P.T. and Bloodborne are completely legal, since they require you to supply your own game files that you bought and dump them from your own console(s). These web-browser-based AAA games, though, do infringe upon copyright law, and can be subject to DMCA takedowns from game developers and publishers any time.

Of course, that doesn't change the fact that these games are compiled into tiny, lightweight WebAssembly packages, meaning that clones of the game will show up faster than the devs can play whack-a-mole with them.

I ran DLSS 5 on Rockstar’s GTA trilogy, and GTA 6 suddenly doesn’t feel that far ahead

Did we get GTA 6 before GTA 6?

3
By  Abhinav Raj

The browser is the new console

It's downright astonishing how dramatically AI is changing the economics of game preservation. For years, recreating a game's engine was a monumental undertaking, reserved only for the most dedicated developers willing to spend months and years, sacrificing any touch of grass. Now, the barrier to entry is dropping fast, and games that seemed destined to remain trapped on aging hardware are finding entirely new ways to reach players.

What's truly fascinating here isn't the legal mess, though. It's that our browsers are quietly turning into gaming platforms in their own right. Without any storefronts or lengthy installations (or even expensive hardware upgrades required), all you need is just a URL and a decent internet connection. The legal battles will continue, but the technical capability is already here, and there's no putting that genie back in the bottle.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The local AI landscape is moving at a breakneck pace. As a matter of fact, it's moving ahead so quickly that anyone on a llama.cpp build from just a couple of months ago could already be behind. New releases continue to bring new features that can change what your hardware is capable of, and sometimes, the gap more often than not means the difference between a model that's usable and a model that's capable.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

If you don't believe me, you need to look no further than the example of the recent developments that have come to Google's family of open-weight models, Gemma 4. Earlier in May, Google shipped multi-token prediction drafters for Gemma models, with llama.cpp adding support for it in June. The drafter happens to be a 242-megabyte file that, on my RTX 4070 Ti Super, boosted Gemma 4 12B from about 75 tokens per second to an average of 179 tokens per second, which is a gain of a whopping 137% across three workloads that I tested myself. Here's how you, too, can make use of it.

My Gemma 4 12B model was fast, but it could be much faster

75 tokens/second was the ceiling, until it wasn't

To establish how fast a model can get, the first step, of course, is to measure how fast it currently runs. I tested my model's baseline speed on my PC with an RTX 4070 Ti Super with 16GB of GDDR6X memory coupled with a Ryzen 5 7600X and 32GB of DDR5 memory first. I served Unsloth's Gemma 4 12B QAT build at the UD-Q4_K_XL quant through llama-server on llama.cpp build b11927, with 32K context, flash attention, every layer on the GPU, and Google's recommended sampler settings (temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 64). In all my tests, I turned the thinking mode off, so that every generated token was counted as a part of an answer.

I gave the model three jobs, including generating a JSON list of fictional PC hardware components, a Python duplicate-file finder, and a short story of 600 words. I gave it the following three prompts in a fresh chat.

  1. Generate a JSON array of 15 fictional PC components. Each object must have these fields: id, name, category, brand, price_usd, release_year, and specs (an object with three fields relevant to the category). Output only the JSON, no commentary.
  2. Write a complete Python command-line tool that recursively scans a directory, finds duplicate files by SHA-256 hash, and prints a report grouped by hash showing each file's path and size. Use argparse, handle permission errors gracefully, and include docstrings. Output only the code.
  3. Write a short story of about 600 words about a lighthouse keeper who slowly realizes the light has been signaling to something out at sea, and that something has started signaling back.

As you can tell, each of these prompts test a unique use-case and represents the prompts users generally send to a model of this size and capability tier. After running each prompt, I recorded the following results. The test methodology comes from the llama.cpp pull request that added Gemma 4 MTP, wherein another tester on the same GPU reported the results in the three categories I've used for the test.

I moved my local models from Ollama to llama.cpp, and the reason I stayed has nothing to do with speed

Convenience beats tokens generated per second, always

2
By  Abhinav Raj

Switching on multi-token prediction took one file and four flags

No new GPU and no smaller models, just a drafter Google made for the purpose

The way that multi-token prediction (MTP) works is by pairing the target model (here, Gemma 4 12B) with a small drafter model that was trained alongside it. Google details this in their documentation, explaining that MTP is the architecture Gemma 4 uses for speculative decoding.

Speculative decoding is essentially a way to get more out of each pass through a large model by letting the small drafter model do the guesswork for token prediction, while the large target model confirms several of those guesses in the time it would normally take to output a single token.

In this case, it means that, rather than having the target model generate every token one at a time, the drafter predicts several tokens ahead, and then, the large model checks all of them in parallel. When a "guess" is rejected by the target model, it still produces the correct token for that position, so the step isn't wasted, and the drafter picks up from there.

For this test, I downloaded both files from Unsloth's Gemma 4 12B QAT repository on Hugging Face, including the UD-Q4_K_XL build and its matching drafter, mtp-gemma-4-12B-it.gguf, which was a conversion of Google's very own drafter. It was important to keep the pair from one repo, because a QAT model should run with its QAT drafter. To switch MTP on, I had to restart llama-server with four additional flags, with everything else from the baseline run kept identical.

I then used four flags: -md mtp-gemma-4-12B-it.gguf (to load the drafter), -ngld 99 (to put the drafter on the GPU alongside the main model), --spec-type draft-mtp (to run the drafter as a Gemma 4 MTP head that reads the main model's cache, rather than a standalone model) and --spec-draft-n-max 3 (which caps each round at three guesses, which is a value I took from similar results on the same GPU in the llama.cpp pull request).

Google AI Pro cost me $20 a month, but Gemma 4 does the same job for free

Farewell, Google AI Pro. Thanks for Gemma 4, Google!

By  Abhinav Raj

Gemma 4 got faster at everything I asked it to write

Code and JSON nearly tripled, and even prose got 73% faster

With the drafter loaded, the only thing left was to run the test again under identical VRAM conditions. There's no other way to put this, besides simply stating that every task got faster. The JSON and code tasks jumped from about 75 tokens per second to around 200, as brackets, field names, and boilerplate are all easy to predict and complemented the drafter-equipped model.

What came as a surprise, however, was the fact that even the prose workload, which gives the drafter more room to miss, ended up running 73% faster.

llama.cpp
See at Official Website

Grab your drafter before you upgrade your GPU

If you run Gemma 4 in llama.cpp, getting a drafter model seems to be one of the easiest and most straightforward ways to get a speed boost for it. All that you need to do is update to the latest build of llama.cpp, download the drafter that matches your model, and add four flags.

The only thing that's worth noting is that dense models like the Gemma 4 12B model I tested benefit from a drafter the most. While I haven't tested any mixture-of-experts models with a drafter yet, Google says that those models benefit less from a drafter on single-user setups. It's also worth noting that the results also vary depending on the specific hardware configuration that you're on, but testers have reported gains on everything from an RTX 5090 to a GT 1030, so there's nothing to lose from giving it a go.

For this test, I downloaded both files from Unsloth's Gemma 4 12B QAT repository on Hugging Face, including the UD-Q4_K_XL build and its matching drafter, mtp-gemma-4-12B-it.gguf, which was a conversion of Google's very own drafter. It was important to keep the pair from one repo, because a QAT model should run with its QAT drafter. To switch MTP on, I had to restart llama-server with four additional flags, with everything else from the baseline run kept identical.

I then used four flags: -md mtp-gemma-4-12B-it.gguf (to load the drafter), -ngld 99 (to put the drafter on the GPU alongside the main model), --spec-type draft-mtp (to run the drafter as a Gemma 4 MTP head that reads the main model's cache, rather than a standalone model) and --spec-draft-n-max 3 (which caps each round at three guesses, which is a value I took from similar results on the same GPU in the llama.cpp pull request).

Google AI Pro cost me $20 a month, but Gemma 4 does the same job for free

Farewell, Google AI Pro. Thanks for Gemma 4, Google!

By  Abhinav Raj

Gemma 4 got faster at everything I asked it to write

Code and JSON nearly tripled, and even prose got 73% faster

With the drafter loaded, the only thing left was to run the test again under identical VRAM conditions. There's no other way to put this, besides simply stating that every task got faster. The JSON and code tasks jumped from about 75 tokens per second to around 200, as brackets, field names, and boilerplate are all easy to predict and complemented the drafter-equipped model.

What came as a surprise, however, was the fact that even the prose workload, which gives the drafter more room to miss, ended up running 73% faster.

item.title: I turned an old router into a travel router, and hotel Wi-Fi finally stopped being annoying
item.itunes:title: I turned an old router into a travel router, and hotel Wi-Fi finally stopped being annoying
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you're traveling with multiple devices like laptops, tablets, phones, and sometimes even streaming sticks, it really exposes the absolute worst of public hospitality networks. Every device requires you to open a browser, hunt down a terms-of-service checkbox, and authenticate through a clunky captive portal splash page. Some hotels enforce strict per-room or per-device connection caps, blocking secondary gadgets or forcing constant re-authentications. A lot of hotels use Layer 2 client isolation to prevent guests from talking to each other, which breaks local file transfers, casting devices, and hardware setups. By repurposing an old wireless router or configuring a dedicated travel networking stack, it can transform how public Wi-Fi is handled by consolidating every personal device behind a single private gateway.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
I turned off 2.4GHz Wi-Fi on my primary SSID, and household smart devices stopped dropping offline

My smart plugs and cameras kept going offline until I split my Wi-Fi into two networks.

20
By  Jasmine Mannan

WISP is the brain behind it all

How does it actually work?

In order to consolidate all of your devices onto a single private gateway, you need to take advantage of WISP, or wireless ISP mode. Instead of plugging the router's WAN port into a physical Ethernet drop, the router's wireless radio operates in client mode to connect directly to your hotel's public Wi-Fi network as its upstream internet source. This essentially allows you to use your router as you would at home, but instead of having it connected directly to a physical port, you can wirelessly connect it to the internet source.

After doing this, you get network address translation and private subnets. The travel router you've created generates its own isolated local subnet, running its own DHCP server and local firewall.

It creates a single upstream client. To the hotel's infrastructure, your entire collection of personal devices appears as a single connected client. It comes up as the travel router's MAC address. You're essentially bypassing arbitrary per-device billing or connection limits as long as you're not capped by a certain amount of data; if you are, all your devices will contribute to that cap since they're connected through the same device.

How to get your travel router set up

You may need to prepare your router in advance

Bypassing captive portals and device limits can be annoying, so make sure you understand the workflow in advance. When first arriving at a hotel, you should connect your travel router to the hotel's Wi-Fi via a wireless ISP mode. Evaluate your old home router's capabilities. If the stock firmware lacks WISP or client bridge modes, flash an open-source networking stack like OpenWRT for granular radio and routing control. WISP mode is necessary to establish local NAT and bypass per-device limits, whereas a pure Layer 2 client bridge can pass hotel DHCP straight through. Once you know you have WISP mode, access the router's management interface, scan for the hotel's SSID via the wireless client interface, and input the shared key and bind it as the WAN uplink.

Next, you need to establish the private access point. You can set up a distinct local SSID and WPA3/WPA2-PSK security passphrase on the router's LAN/WLAN interface, ensuring a familiar network name and password that you can easily recognize amongst a lot of different wireless connections that may appear in your hotel.

Once you've set up Wisp, this doesn't actually bypass any of the hotel's captive portals. You have to connect a single device, like your phone or laptop, to your travel router's private Wi-Fi network. When you attempt to browse the web, it will redirect traffic through the hotel's captive portal login page. Authenticate as normal, and once you've done this, the router's WAN interface should be granted internet access. After this, you should get instantaneous downstream connectivity because the travel router handles the upstream authentication session.

All other devices connected to your private travel SSID immediately gain internet access without ever needing to touch the hotel splash page. In scenarios where hotel portals tie access to specific device MAC addresses or require explicit wired Ethernet registration, some travel routers can clone your laptop's MAC address to seamlessly clear network access controls.

You get a lot of perks

From security to no more client isolation

One of the main benefits of using this method is being able to bypass any Layer 2 client isolation. Layer 2 isolation enforced by hotels can prevent your devices from talking to one another, but these only affect the router's WAN interface in this instance. This means that all of your local devices that are connected to your travel router remain fully visible to each other within your private travel subnet, allowing secure local file sharing and remote access without any interference.

Alongside this, you get a lot of security benefits too. Hotel networks are notorious hotbeds for unencrypted traffic sniffing, ARP spoofing, and man-in-the-middle attacks across shared local subnets. Because you're using your own private network, you can actually have encapsulated tunneling by routing your travel router's traffic through a persistent WireGuard or OpenVPN tunnel back to your home server or a trusted VPS. This method neutralizes those public packet inspections.

Get rid of hotel captive portals

Use hotel Wi-Fi just as you would at home

Battling hotel captive portals and device limits natively on every gadget introduces unnecessary administrative friction and security exposure. Repurposing an old router into a WISP gateway centralizes authentication and restores local network control. Stop wrestling with hospitality network restrictions device by device. Configure an old router with client mode routing, encapsulate your traffic behind a private NAT firewall, and make public Wi-Fi behave like your home network.

item.title: Someone got Pokémon Pokopia running on a PS5 with Linux on it, and I don't know what to believe anymore
item.itunes:title: Someone got Pokémon Pokopia running on a PS5 with Linux on it, and I don't know what to believe anymore
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Pokemon Pokopia runs on a PS5 running Linux — a wild, layered port.
  • Graphics are hit-or-miss: the early build shows shadowy characters.
  • Decompiles and ports keep expanding what's possible — the sky seems to be the limit.

Have you ever had those moments where you see something develop and think, "That's incredible, but there's no way someone can top that," only for someone to top it?

Well, I had that exact thought when our Patrick O'Rourke, XDA's News and Entertainment Editor, reported on people porting Super Mario Bros. Wonder over to the PC, because how do you get better than that? it turns out, there is one way: getting Pokémon Pokopia to run on a PS5, which, in turn, is running Linux.

Is it a PC port of a PS5 port, or both? Who knows?

Pokémon Pokopia on a PS5 on Linux is the weirdest thing you'll see today

This one's got layers

Over on the @CentroLeaks X feed (via VideoCardz), there's a video of someone getting Pokémon Pokopia running on the PS5. Not only that, but the PS5 is running Linux, making this an interesting example of how people are getting Nintendo games on other consoles.

So, how well does it run? Well, right now, it's still a work in progress. The video below shows the game running, but all the characters are just shadowy figures.

Meanwhile, there's also been progress on getting ProsperoEden, an unofficial port of the Eden emulator to PS5, to work with Pokémon Pokopia. There's a video showing everything looking properly textured, with the framerate looking a little slow

Still, it's pretty impressive to see how far things have come. With all these decompilations and ports, who knows what games we'll see on platforms they normally shouldn't run on? Right now, the sky seems to be the limit.

I put a Raspberry Pi inside my Nintendo 3DS, and now my PC sees it as a gamepad, webcam, and microphone

The DSpico can turn your DS into an impressive bag of tricks.

5
By  Adam Conway

item.title: Your CPU has less than 4.2ms to keep up at 240FPS, and that's harder than it sounds
item.itunes:title: Your CPU has less than 4.2ms to keep up at 240FPS, and that's harder than it sounds
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've spent enough time tweaking settings in competitive shooters to know that simply turning everything down to Low doesn't automatically guarantee the frame rates I'm trying to hit. I used to blame my GPU whenever my FPS fell short, and while that logic makes sense when you're playing demanding AAA titles at 1440p or 4K, it doesn't necessarily hold up when you're chasing 200+FPS in esports titles. At some point, the CPU becomes the limiting factor, and even a faster GPU isn't going to move the needle.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

It all comes down to how quickly your CPU can prepare frames for the GPU to render. When you're gaming at 60FPS, your PC needs to deliver a new frame every 16.7ms, which modern CPUs can handle without breaking a sweat. Even at 120FPS, when that window drops to 8.3ms, most CPUs can keep up just fine. But at 240FPS, you're down to just 4.17ms, and that's when even flagship gaming CPUs from a few years ago can struggle to maintain that pace. At these frame rates, your CPU matters just as much as your GPU, if not more.

3 things I wish I knew before pairing an older CPU with a flagship GPU

A flagship GPU means nothing without the right CPU

By  Hamlin Rozario

A faster GPU won't make your CPU prepare frames faster

And that's why lowering graphics settings doesn't help after a point

The thing is, your GPU isn't the only component doing work when you're playing a game. Sure, at higher resolutions in demanding titles, you could say it does most of the heavy lifting, but even then, your CPU still has to handle things like game logic, physics, and player movements before the GPU can render a frame. The only difference is that at lower frame rates, your CPU has more time to get through all that work. At 200+FPS, though, it has to do the same kind of work much more frequently, and there's only so much it can process in a tighter window.

When your CPU struggles to keep up, your GPU ends up waiting, and that's essentially what a CPU bottleneck is. At this point, lowering graphics settings or even enabling upscaling will barely improve your FPS because your GPU isn't what's holding back performance. In fact, that may just reduce GPU usage while your FPS stays in the same ballpark. And if that's happening with your current GPU, upgrading it isn't going to solve the problem either.

Maintaining 240FPS is a lot harder than hitting it

Your 1% lows and frame-time spikes can reveal CPU limitations

When we're benchmarking games, we tend to focus too much on the average FPS because that's the easiest way to judge performance. But that doesn't really tell us how consistently a game runs. That's why it's important to look at other metrics like 1% lows and frame times, especially when you're trying to maintain 240FPS. You could be averaging 240FPS in a competitive shooter like Apex Legends, but that doesn't mean your frame rate isn't dropping well below that number when things get hectic.

Maintaining 240FPS means keeping your frame times consistently around 4.17ms, but that's easier said than done. If your CPU takes longer to prepare a frame for the GPU to render, that can show up in the frame-time graph as a spike. You may experience stutters or hitches when that happens, even if your average FPS looks fine. Then, you have 1% lows, which represent performance during the slowest 1% of frames. If you're averaging 240FPS but your 1% lows are closer to 100FPS, that's a clear sign your frame delivery isn't nearly as consistent as the average suggests.

Falling short isn't going to ruin your experience, though

But if you're chasing a consistent 240FPS, CPU performance should be your priority

It's not like you need to maintain 240FPS at all times to enjoy competitive shooters. Even if your frame rate occasionally drops to 180FPS, you're still getting a pretty smooth experience for the most part. Sure, you may feel those dips, but that's not going to suddenly make a game unplayable or put you at a significant disadvantage during a gunfight. As long as the CPU bottleneck isn't significant enough to cause frequent stutters or major FPS drops, I wouldn't obsess too much over it.

But if you're like me and you're sensitive to changes in responsiveness, you're going to notice that dip from 240FPS to 180FPS more than most people. Anyone who plays competitive shooters seriously can probably relate to this. Consistency matters a lot in games like these, and the last thing you want is your frame rate dropping during intense moments. That's why I'd still prioritize a faster CPU if I'm trying to consistently hit 240FPS or higher in the games I play. At these frame rates, your CPU can very well be the difference between occasionally hitting your FPS target and maintaining it.

The fastest CPUs are for those chasing the highest frame rates

There's a reason why CPUs like the 9800X3D sell like hotcakes. It's not like you need that kind of processing power to play AAA titles at 4K. If anything, even my old 5800X3D held up pretty well in those scenarios. But if you're after the absolute best frame rates, having one of the fastest gaming CPUs can make a noticeable difference, especially when games become CPU-bound at lower resolutions or when using DLSS. Even an RTX 5090 can only do so much when the CPU starts holding it back.

The thing is, your GPU isn't the only component doing work when you're playing a game. Sure, at higher resolutions in demanding titles, you could say it does most of the heavy lifting, but even then, your CPU still has to handle things like game logic, physics, and player movements before the GPU can render a frame. The only difference is that at lower frame rates, your CPU has more time to get through all that work. At 200+FPS, though, it has to do the same kind of work much more frequently, and there's only so much it can process in a tighter window.

When your CPU struggles to keep up, your GPU ends up waiting, and that's essentially what a CPU bottleneck is. At this point, lowering graphics settings or even enabling upscaling will barely improve your FPS because your GPU isn't what's holding back performance. When we're benchmarking games, we tend to focus too much on the average FPS because that's the easiest way to judge performance. But that doesn't really tell us how consistently a game runs. That's why it's important to look at other metrics like 1% lows and frame times, especially when you're trying to maintain 240FPS. You could be averaging 240FPS in a competitive shooter like Apex Legends, but that doesn't mean your frame rate isn't dropping well below that number when things get hectic.

Maintaining 240FPS means keeping your frame times consistently around 4.17ms, but that's easier said than done. If your CPU takes longer to prepare a frame for the GPU to render, that can show up in the frame-time graph as a spike. You may experience stutters or hitches when that happens, even if your average FPS looks fine. Then, you have 1% lows, which represent performance during the slowest 1% of frames. If you're averaging 240FPS but your 1% lows are closer to 100FPS, that's a clear sign your frame delivery isn't nearly as consistent as the average suggests.

Falling short isn't going to ruin your experience, though

But if you're chasing a consistent 240FPS, CPU performance should be your priority

It's not like you need to maintain 240FPS at all times to enjoy competitive shooters. Even if your frame rate occasionally drops to 180FPS, you're still getting a pretty smooth experience for the most part. Sure, you may feel those dips, but that's not going to suddenly make a game unplayable or put you at a significant disadvantage during a gunfight. As long as the CPU bottleneck isn't significant enough to cause frequent stutters or major FPS drops, I wouldn't obsess too much over it.

But if you're like me and you're sensitive to changes in responsiveness, you're going to notice that dip from 240FPS to 180FPS more than most people. Anyone who plays competitive shooters seriously can probably relate to this. Consistency matters a lot in games like these, and the last thing you want is your frame rate dropping during intense moments. That's why I'd still prioritize a faster CPU if I'm trying to consistently hit 240FPS or higher in the games I play. At these frame rates, your CPU can very well be the difference between occasionally hitting your FPS target and maintaining it.

The fastest CPUs are for those chasing the highest frame rates

There's a reason why CPUs like the 9800X3D sell like hotcakes. It's not like you need that kind of processing power to play AAA titles at 4K. If anything, even my old 5800X3D held up pretty well in those scenarios. But if you're after the absolute best frame rates, having one of the fastest gaming CPUs can make a noticeable difference, especially when games become CPU-bound at lower resolutions or when using DLSS. Even an RTX 5090 can only do so much when the CPU starts holding it back.
